#10626. MIT scientists build a tiny robot that swims using living muscle cells

A swimming robot does not necessarily need a bulky motor or powerful mechanical parts to move through water. MIT researchers have demonstrated that a single, carefully engineered layer of living muscle cells can generate enough force to propel a tiny robot forward.

The engineers developed an extremely thin swimming robot that uses living muscle tissue to move its fins. Described in a new study published in Advanced Functional Materials, the device has a flexible gel framework roughly the length and width of a stick of gum. The gel forms two fins, each coated with a layer of muscle cells far thinner than a human hair. These cells have been genetically modified to contract when exposed to light.

By directing light onto either fin, the researchers can trigger muscle contractions that make the fin flap and push the robot through water. Adjusting which fin receives light and how frequently it is illuminated allows the team to control both its speed and direction.

In experiments, the remarkably thin robot successfully swam and turned through a simple underwater maze. At maximum speed, it covered approximately four times its body length per minute. Although that is much slower than an Olympic swimmer, who can travel up to 65 body lengths per minute, it is comparable to the swimming pace of a cow shark moving leisurely through the ocean.

"It takes a lot of force to move through water versus air," says study author Ritu Raman, associate professor of mechanical engineering at MIT. "The robot's quite strong, given its size. "

A New Generation of Robots Powered by Living Muscle

The device represents the first demonstration of a very thin, two-dimensional robot that can move from place to place using living muscle tissue.

Most existing biohybrid robots rely on relatively large, three-dimensional structures made from laboratory-grown skeletal muscle. Producing these structures typically requires millions of cells. Raman explains that thinner designs could reduce manufacturing costs while potentially improving movement efficiency.

"Currently, biohybrid robots from our group and others' are built from bulky, 3D chunks of lab-grown skeletal muscle that require millions of cells to fabricate," says Raman, who notes that thinner, less bulky designs such as the team's new bot could be cheaper to build and could move more efficiently. "We believe that biohybrid robots powered by living muscle could one day perform delicate jobs like exploring environments too fragile or unpredictable for conventional hardware, because living tissue is soft, responsive to its surroundings, and can heal itself."

The MIT research team also included first author Maheera Bawa, along with Arielle Berman, Laura Schwendeman, Ferdows Afghah, and Seanbiron Johnson.

From Artificial Muscle to a Swimming Robot

The new swimming robot builds on an earlier achievement by Raman's laboratory. Last year, the researchers created an artificial muscle disk inspired by the human iris, demonstrating how a thin layer of living cells could produce precisely controlled movements.

For that project, the engineers patterned a gel disk with grooves extending outward from its center and forming concentric circles. They then placed living muscle cells on the surface, where the cells grew into a thin layer following the patterned channels.

When illuminated, the muscle tissue contracted in different directions, causing the disk to stretch and compress. Its movements resembled the way the iris of the human eye changes shape as the pupil expands or narrows.

The experiment established that researchers could grow extremely thin muscle layers in intricate arrangements and use light to control their movements along multiple directions.

"People hadn't seen this muscle architecture engineered from scratch before," Raman says. "And the cells were moving in multiple directions. But they only moved about 100 microns. From a robotics perspective, their movements were tiny."

For the latest project, the researchers wanted to dramatically increase the amount of movement and force generated by the muscle cells. Their goal was to produce contractions powerful enough to propel a robot through water.

They determined that achieving this would require a better foundation for the living muscle tissue.

The earlier artificial iris had used fibrin, an exceptionally soft gel, as its underlying structure. However, the team found that fibrin could quickly shrink under the forces exerted by contracting muscle cells, limiting the effectiveness of the resulting movement.

To overcome this problem, the engineers investigated three characteristics of the gel foundation: its chemical composition, its stiffness, and the dimensions and geometry of the grooves used to organize muscle growth.

"For engineering any type of tissue, it's known that these are knobs you can tune," Raman says. "And we wanted to optimize all these parameters to support live muscle cells."

Engineering a Stronger Muscle-Powered Robot

Finding the right supporting material required testing gels with different formulations, stiffness levels, and surface patterns.

The researchers compared several groove shapes, including narrow channels with square profiles and longer channels with curved bottoms. They discovered that muscle cells aligned more effectively inside square-shaped grooves.

This alignment was important because muscle cells that grow in the same direction are more likely to merge into fibers. Those fibers can then form stronger muscle tissue that contracts in a coordinated way. The square grooves therefore provided a more effective structure for producing force.

The team also replaced fibrin with gelatin methacrylate (GelMA), a material commonly used to grow and engineer biological tissue.

By adjusting the formulation of GelMA, the researchers produced supporting gels with varying degrees of stiffness. They then examined how muscle cells developed on each surface and measured their ability to generate force.

Stiffer gels produced the best results. On these firmer surfaces, muscle cells grew in better alignment and generated stronger contractions.

The engineers next investigated how thick the gel should be. They determined that a film measuring approximately half a millimeter offered an effective balance. It was sturdy enough to support a single layer of muscle cells while remaining sufficiently lightweight to prevent the contracting cells from detaching from the surface.

The team further improved muscle performance through a form of exercise. Repeated pulses of light stimulated the cells to contract, strengthening the muscle tissue before it was incorporated into the swimming robot.

With the gel structure optimized and the muscle cells strengthened, the researchers assembled their swimming device.

The finished robot consisted of a thin gel framework divided into two fins. Both sides of the gel were patterned with square-bottomed grooves and covered with living muscle cells. As the cells developed, they fused into organized muscle fibers capable of contracting together.

Each fin could be activated independently using light, giving the researchers a simple way to control the robot's movements.

"You can think of the robot as having two independent muscles," Raman says. "If we shine a light on just one, only that muscle moves. If shining on both, they both flap."

To test the device, the researchers placed it inside a large petri dish filled with water. They then moved a light source by hand, illuminating the fins to guide the robot through a maze positioned inside the dish.

As the muscles contracted, the fins flapped and propelled the robot through the water. By changing the light stimulation, the engineers successfully controlled its movement and helped it navigate the obstacles.

Although the robot demonstrated the ability to swim and steer, its current shape remains relatively simple. The primary objective of the experiment was to establish that an exceptionally thin layer of engineered muscle tissue could generate enough force for swimming.

The researchers now plan to refine the robot's body to improve its speed. Beyond demonstrating a new approach to biohybrid robotics, the technology could eventually be useful for monitoring aquatic environments or operating in locations where conventional rigid machines might cause damage.

"Our next goal is to optimize the body design to enable faster swimming," Raman says. "But even at slow swim speeds, one could imagine a muscle-powered swimmer being used for purposes like environmental monitoring in aquatic environments."

The Office of Naval Research provided partial funding for this research.

#10624. FAA grounds all flights in the U.S. until further notice: Reports cite air traffic control outage

In a rare move, the Federal Aviation Administration said Friday that it was grounding all flights in the United States from departing “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety . . . until further notice,” according to NBC News.

The FAA reportedly issued the ground stop “due to several impacts to ATC [air traffic control] Frequencies and/or Radar capabilities,” with the FAA command center telling airlines it does not have further information on the “timing or cause of this outage,” aviation industry news service The Air Current reported.

Reached by Fast Company, the FAA pointed to a post on X from Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy, saying the ground stop “follows a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.”

Duffy added: “FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them.”

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House, “there is no indication that we’ve had, no reason to believe, that as of right now this was a threat to the United States,” later adding, “this was a telecommunication outage,” per CNN.

According to FlightAware.com, a live flight tracker website, there are more than 9,000 flights delayed within, into, or out of the U.S. today, with 440 flights canceled (as of 5:20 p.m. ET).

“Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis,” the FAA posted on X.

The last nationwide ground stop was on January 11, 2023, when a contractor for the FAA “unintentionally deleted files related to a key pilot safety system,” according to CNN reporting at that time. The only other time such an order was issued was following the attacks on September 11, 2001.

#10622. Apple TV has a new ASL feature, offering a richer language experience beyond captions

Apple introduced a new sign language interpretation feature on Friday, alongside the premiere of the Apple TV movie Being Heumann.

The feature, designed with native signers, offers a visual of a person on the screen. Rather than replacing captions as an accessibility option, Apple is offering another function to improve users’ viewing experience through American Sign Language and British Sign Language.

People in the Deaf community have cited inability to get the full experience of watching shows and movies due to captions that lack descriptions of tone and mood. Poorly timed captions can throw off an entire episode or movie, and incorrect language can alter the understanding of a conversation.

The new feature goes hand in hand with the 2026 biographical drama directed by Sian Heder based on the memoir Being Heumann: An Unrepentant Memoir of a Disability Rights Activist by its namesake Judith Heumann with writer Kristen Joiner.

Starring Mark Ruffalo and Dylan O’Brien, and Ruth Madeley as Heumann, the film debuted in select theaters on November 6 and was released for streaming on Apple TV today. 

A 2021 Census Bureau presentation discussed the difficulty of collecting accurate ASL-user statistics through traditional household language surveys. The Deaf community is often undercounted in national data, making it harder to measure accessibility needs. 

Apple Originals have led the industry in providing accessibility features, such as Subtitles for the Deaf and Hard of Hearing and Audio Description for blind and low-vision audiences, in multiple languages, worldwide. 

For its new feature, Apple created each interpretation with a DASL (director of artistic sign language) and an interpreter. They worked together in a studio to create high-quality sign language, capturing the tone and emotional intensity of each film being interpreted.

“I’m proud to have been part of Being Heumann and thrilled to see Apple TV supporting greater accessibility for Deaf audiences,” said Daniel Durant, who appears in the movie and also directed the film’s sign language interpretation.

#10621. Cambridge scientists create a $10 chip that could put a medical lab on your wrist

A new optical sensor costing just $10 could bring laboratory-level precision to wearable health monitors, potentially allowing people to track blood glucose without needles. The technology could also transform food testing, industrial quality control, and environmental monitoring.

Researchers at the University of Cambridge and GlitterinTech (a start-up founded by the same research group) have developed a new type of optical spectrometer that combines exceptional accuracy with a remarkably small size and low cost. Measuring just centimeters across, the device could be incorporated into portable electronics and wearable health technology. Its potential applications range from monitoring important health markers in real time to identifying materials and detecting changes in chemical composition.

Optical spectrometers work by analyzing light to reveal information about the substances it interacts with. They are essential tools in medicine, manufacturing, chemical testing, and environmental research. However, making these instruments smaller has traditionally meant compromising their performance. Compact spectrometers often have limited measurement ranges, reduced resolution, or lower accuracy, making them better suited to identifying substances than performing precise measurements.

The researchers believe their new design could overcome these limitations. Known as a convolutional spectrometer, it uses a mathematical principle called the convolution theorem to analyze light in a fundamentally different way. According to the team, this approach delivers performance that surpasses existing types of spectrometers in several key areas, including designs based on light dispersion, Fourier transforms, and computational reconstruction.

A New Way to Analyze Light With Extraordinary Precision

Traditional spectrometers generally separate incoming light into its component wavelengths or use complex calculations to reconstruct its spectrum. The new device takes another approach by performing a mathematical operation called convolution directly on the incoming light.

To accomplish this, the researchers arranged optical components with repeating spectral responses in a sequence. These components can include unbalanced Mach-Zehnder interferometers or micro-ring resonators. By adjusting them in proportion to one another, the system can shift its response to different wavelengths in a controlled, linear fashion. Fast Fourier transforms are then used to accurately recover the light spectrum.

"The key insight was to go back to the mathematics and ask whether there was a fundamentally cleaner way to retrieve spectra," said Dr. Chunhui Yao, a lead author of the study. "By using the convolution theorem directly in the optical domain, we avoid many of the limitations that have held miniaturized spectrometers back. This gives us high precision, strong noise tolerance, and very low computational overhead, all in a compact and low-cost system."

The researchers built the spectrometer using a silicon nitride photonic platform and integrated it with onboard electronics. It operates across a broad range of near-infrared wavelengths (1200-1700 nm) and can collect and process measurements in less than a second.

Another important advantage is its ability to expand its measurement capabilities without major hardware changes. Because the system uses repeating optical patterns, its spectral bandwidth can theoretically be extended almost without limit. Adding more optical components in sequence can also increase its resolution exponentially.

A $10 Sensor That Could Transform Food Testing and Healthcare

To evaluate the device outside purely theoretical measurements, the researchers tested it on a variety of materials and substances. The results demonstrated its potential for applications that normally depend on larger, more expensive laboratory instruments.

When used to identify plastics, pharmaceuticals, coffee, flour, and tea, the spectrometer achieved a 100% classification success rate in the reported tests. It also measured concentrations in water-based and organic solutions with accuracies of approximately 0.01%, exceeding the performance of commercial benchtop spectrometers in those experiments.

The healthcare demonstrations were particularly promising. Under conditions designed to reflect real physiological environments, the device accurately measured several human biomarkers, including skin moisture, blood alcohol, blood lactate, and blood glucose.

The researchers also demonstrated noninvasive glucose tracking over an extended period in one participant. Although further testing would be needed before the technology could become a practical medical product, the finding suggests a possible route toward monitoring blood sugar without repeatedly piercing the skin.

"These biomedical demonstrations are particularly exciting," said Prof. Qixiang Cheng, who led the project. "What makes this work stand out is not just performance in the lab, but technical readiness. Dr. Chunhui Yao's contribution was crucial in translating a mathematical concept into a fully packaged, robust system that operates reliably across temperature extremes and real-world conditions. That combination is what opens the door to practical deployment."

The sensor also demonstrated impressive resistance to temperature changes. It continued operating reliably between -20°C and 80°C, an unusually wide temperature range for a miniature spectrometer. This durability could be especially valuable for wearable devices, factory equipment, and sensors operating outdoors.

Why a Simpler Design Could Be a Major Breakthrough

The new spectrometer's advantages extend beyond its accuracy, size, and price. Its internal design also reduces the amount of computing power needed to analyze incoming light.

Many existing miniature spectrometers depend on complicated calibration procedures and demanding algorithms to reconstruct spectral information. These methods can become unreliable when measurements contain noise, and they often require substantial processing resources.

The Cambridge team's convolution-based approach avoids much of this complexity. Because the measurements follow a linear mathematical relationship, the system can recover spectra rapidly and consistently while using relatively little computational power.

"This is a beautiful example of how elegant engineering can unlock real impact," said Prof. Richard Penty, who contributed to the photonic system design and integration. "The architecture is simple, scalable, and manufacturable, yet it delivers precision that rivals or exceeds much larger instruments. Dr. Chunhui Yao played a central role in bringing together the photonic design, system integration, and experimental validation that made this possible."

Its relatively simple construction could also make the technology easier to manufacture on a large scale, potentially bringing sophisticated optical measurements to devices where conventional spectrometers would be too bulky or expensive.

Bringing Laboratory-Grade Measurements to Everyday Devices

The researchers envision a future in which accurate optical sensing becomes a routine feature of everyday technology rather than something largely confined to specialized laboratories.

In industrial settings, inexpensive spectrometers could be installed throughout manufacturing facilities to continuously check material composition and product quality. Similar sensors could monitor food freshness, identify substances, and analyze environmental conditions on a much larger scale than is currently practical.

Healthcare could see equally significant changes. Compact sensors might eventually enable wearables to measure hydration levels, detect signs of alcohol intoxication, track biomarkers related to physical fitness, or continuously monitor glucose levels for people managing diabetes.

"Our vision is to make spectrometry as ubiquitous as temperature or motion sensing," added Prof. Qixiang Cheng. "This work shows that high-quality spectral information doesn't have to be confined to the laboratory -- it can be embedded directly into the technologies people use every day."

As photonic technology becomes smaller and more advanced, the convolutional spectrometer provides a promising example of how mathematical insights and practical engineering can make sophisticated scientific instruments simpler, cheaper, and more accessible. By combining high precision with a device that costs around $10, the researchers have opened a potential path toward a new generation of smart sensors capable of measuring the hidden chemistry of our bodies and surroundings.

Materials provided by University of Cambridge. Original written by Michael Shuff. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#10620. This simple QR code creator is all about your privacy

QR codes are popping up everywhere these days, and for good reason. They have all kinds of practical uses, from replacing your business card and collecting cashless payments to linking to menus or information on museum exhibits. But creating one can be a pain.

Search online for “QR code creator,” and you’ll run into sluggish websites with annoying banner ads, sign-up walls, and invasive privacy policies. Some even hijack your links with their own tracking code.

It really shouldn’t be this complicated.

Fortunately, today’s tool introduces a new way to create QR codes that’s refreshingly simple—and it comes from a source with a strong track record of keeping your data private. 

This tip originally appeared in the free Cool Tools newsletter from The Intelligence. Get the next issue in your inbox and get ready to discover all sorts of awesome tech treasures!

The simplest QR code creator

A little refresher before getting to the tool itself: QR codes are those square-shaped barcodes full of little pixelated squares and a set of larger markers in the corners. You might see them in restaurants (“Leave us a review on Yelp!”), from street vendors collecting Venmo payments, or as part of the setup process for a smart home device. Most of the time, scanning them just opens a link to a web page without your having to type anything.

➜ For a simple, straightforward way to create your own QR codes with ease, check out Ente QR, a free website with no sign-ups or usage limits.

⌚ Generating a code takes mere seconds, and only a few minutes longer if you want to customize the look.

There are any number of reasons why you might find it helpful to create QR codes of your own. I keep an image file with a QR code handy on my phone, for instance, to let folks easily sign up for my newsletters. You could also have a QR code that links to your website on business cards, a printout of one that points people to a shared digital photo album for your next party, or to a page with your Wi-Fi password and other details for house guests.

✅ Whatever you want to use it for, Ente QR lets you create a code with a few simple steps:

  • Paste a link into the address field.
  • Tweak the color and visual style of the QR code.
  • Click the download button to get the QR code image as a PNG image file.

The site’s customization features strike the right balance between simplicity and utility, with a handful of dot formatting options and preset colors, plus a color picker if you want something specific. There’s also a “Logo” option that embeds an image in the middle of the QR code.

Ente says the QR code creation runs entirely in your browser, and the codes always lead directly to the link you included, with no creepy tracking in between. It’s a side project from a company that mainly works on private photo and document storage. 

The biggest limitation is that Ente’s QR codes are only for linking to web addresses. If you want to create a QR code for sharing plain text, a prefilled email, or a digital contact card, BlockSurvey’s privacy-focused QR code generator is a good alternative. While it’s not as stylish as Ente QR, it supports more data formats—but for most people’s purposes, Ente more than fits the bill.

  • Ente QR is available in any browser and works well on both desktop and mobile devices.
  • It’s free to use with no ads, sign-ups, subscriptions, or usage limits.
  • Ente does not track the URLs in the QR codes you create and does not set tracking cookies on its website.

#10619. Prompt Management in TypeScript: LangSmith vs Git vs 3 Open-Source Registries

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Every prompt registry we tested can change a prompt in a running TypeScript app, roll it back, and give production and staging different versions. LangSmith's prompt hub, Langfuse, Phoenix and AcruxCore all passed those three tests. The real differences show up elsewhere: which template syntax each one accepts, how many npm packages it pulls in, how long a change takes to reach the app, and what happens when the registry is down.

We tested all of this with one small app and one prompt, which has a condition and a loop. Git files served as the baseline. Every number below comes from a recorded run.

Most teams start with prompts in code: a template string, or a .txt file next to the code that uses it. That works until a product manager wants to change one sentence, and the change has to wait for a full release.

A prompt registry moves the text out of the deploy. The app fetches the prompt by name and by a label such as production. You change which version the label points to, and the app picks up the new text without a deploy.

LangSmith's prompt hub is the best-known registry, but it is not the only one. Several of the LangSmith alternatives also manage prompts, and three of them are open source and self-hostable: Langfuse, Phoenix and AcruxCore. We covered how those tools handle tracing in Self-Hosted LangSmith Alternatives: 4 Tools Tested on One TypeScript Agent. This article covers prompts only.

Every tool got the same prompt, support-reply. Its template takes three variables: a customer name, a plan, and a list of help articles. It has one condition: a priority line appears only for premium customers. It also has one loop: one line per help article. In Jinja2 syntax, the template looks like this:

One help article contains the text Settings > Export. We included it on purpose, to catch any tool that HTML-escapes > into >.

Every tool then ran the same sequence from a TypeScript script:

Each tool used its own documented TypeScript SDK. The four registries passed all six steps. The rest of this article covers how each one got there, and what it cost.

Keeping prompts in the repository costs almost nothing. The template sits in prompts/support-reply.njk, and nunjucks, the JavaScript port of Jinja2, renders it:

The autoescape: false line matters. Our first version called nunjucks.renderString() directly, and the test failed. The default environment HTML-escapes its output, so Settings > Export reached the model as Settings > Export. Escaping is correct for web pages and wrong for prompts.

Git gives you full Jinja2, code review on every prompt change, and history in the same place as the code. What it can't do is change a prompt in a running app. Every edit, and every rollback, waits for a deploy.

LangSmith stores a prompt as a serialized LangChain object (ChatPromptTemplate), not as plain text. LangSmith's own documentation says you must use the LangChain npm package to pull prompts in TypeScript (Manage prompts programmatically). So a plain TypeScript app that uses the openai package still needs langchain and @langchain/core:

Those three packages installed 23 packages and 70 MB. Most of the size is @langchain/* (27 MB) and js-tiktoken (22 MB).

Templates. In TypeScript, LangChain accepts f-string and mustache templates. Mustache sections ({{#docs}}…{{/docs}}) handled our loop. Mustache has no ==, though, so the premium check became an is_premium boolean computed in code. We also tried templateFormat: "jinja2", which LangChain's Python package supports. In TypeScript it threw DEFAULT_PARSER_MAPPING[templateFormat] is not a function.

Labels and rollback. production and staging are reserved tags, and the documentation moves them in the UI. The langsmith JavaScript client has no public method that moves a tag. Our script called the same REST route the SDK uses internally (POST /api/v1/repos/-//tags). It worked, but it is not a documented API.

Caching. The SDK caches prompts for 300 seconds by default. In our test, a running app saw the new version 300 seconds after we moved the tag.

Langfuse's TypeScript client is one package, @langfuse/client. It installed 5 packages and 8 MB:

Creating a version, moving a label and reading by label are all public SDK calls: prompt.create, prompt.update and prompt.get (Get started with prompt management).

Templates. The documentation shows only {{variable}} substitution. But compile() calls the mustache library, so sections worked for our loop. The type signature accepts only string values, so passing a list needed a cast. The Langfuse UI colours the section tags red, and it lists title and body as the prompt's variables, not docs or is_premium. We would not depend on behaviour the documentation doesn't promise. When we sent the Jinja2 version instead, Langfuse returned the {% if %} and {% for %} tags unchanged, with no error. The model would have received them as text.

Caching. The cache time is 60 seconds by default (Caching). Our app saw the change after 62 seconds. Langfuse is also the only client with a fallback option: a prompt string the SDK uses when it cannot reach the server on a cold start.

Phoenix's TypeScript client fetches a prompt by name and tag, and toSDK() converts it into the message format the openai package expects. Phoenix templates only replace variables, so the condition and the loop have to run in your code before rendering:

That is 16 lines, against 6 to 8 for the other registries. All the extra lines are template logic that now lives in the app.

Templates. Phoenix offers MUSTACHE, F_STRING and NONE formats (Prompts reference). Even in MUSTACHE mode, though, rendering is a plain replacement of {{name}}. When we sent mustache sections, they came back unchanged, with no error.

Errors. getPrompt() catches every error, logs it and returns null. You can see this in the client source, src/utils/getPromptBySelector.ts. A missing prompt and an unreachable server look the same to your code, which is why the snippet checks for null.

Size and caching. The client installed 57 packages and 90 MB. Most of that is OpenTelemetry, which comes in through its @arizeai/phoenix-otel dependency. The client has no prompt cache, so every render is a network call. That is also why a label change showed up immediately: 0 seconds in our test.

AcruxCore stores Jinja2 templates and renders them on the server with nunjucks. The SDK sends the variables and gets back finished messages:

The template from the test section works as it is, condition and loop included, with no is_premium flag computed in code. A label is called an alias here, and promoteAlias() moves it (Manage prompts via the SDK). The SDK installed 3 packages and 12 MB. Most of the 12 MB is one OpenTelemetry package, @opentelemetry/semantic-conventions.

Templates. Jinja2 only. When we committed the mustache version, AcruxCore rejected it at commit time with Template parse error: unexpected token: #. That is a clear error, but it also means that moving mustache prompts from LangSmith or Langfuse requires rewriting them.

We sent the same two templates, a Jinja2 one and a mustache one, to each tool's own renderer:

The rows that matter most are the ones where the tags were left in the output, because those failures produce no error. The model receives raw template syntax, and the only symptom is a strange answer. Whatever tool you pick, test one prompt with logic in it before you move the rest.

Putting logic in the template is not automatically better. It lets someone change the condition without a deploy. It also lets them break the condition without a deploy. Keeping logic in code, as Phoenix forces you to do, puts every branch under code review and in your tests.

A registry is a new runtime dependency, so we tested an outage. The app reached each registry through a local proxy, and we switched the proxy off. A separate process then started while the registry was still unreachable.

LangSmith, Langfuse and AcruxCore keep serving the last good version while the registry is down, even after the cache time has passed. The risk is a cold start: a new container or a serverless function that boots during the outage. Langfuse's fallback option is the built-in answer to that. With the other tools, keep a copy of each prompt in your code as a fallback, which brings back part of the Git setup.

Keep prompts in Git if engineers make every prompt change and your deploys are quick. Set autoescape: false, and you get Jinja2, reviews and history for free.

Use LangSmith's prompt hub if you already use LangChain, or already trace with LangSmith. If your app doesn't use LangChain, budget for the extra dependency and for the tag moves that only the UI supports.

Use Langfuse if you want a small client, a local compile(), and a fallback for cold starts. Keep to {{variable}} substitution unless you are comfortable relying on mustache behaviour that the documentation doesn't promise.

Use Phoenix if you already use it for tracing, or if you prefer all template logic in code. Remember the null check, and that every render is a network call.

Use AcruxCore if you want real conditions and loops in the template and rendering on the server. Expect one network call per new set of variables, and a personal API key for writes.

Before you choose, run one of your own prompts with real logic in it through the tool's SDK, not through its playground. Two of the four registries we tested failed on template syntax without any error, and an SDK run is where you would see that.

#10617. A New York Times writer spent an hour trying to reach Walmart. Then she deleted her account and told the world

When your AI tool for customer service causes so much frustration that it’s featured in the nation’s largest newspaper, you know you’ve got a problem. That’s where Walmart finds itself this week. 

The leading brick-and-mortar retailer, and second-biggest company on earth by revenue (recently edged out by Amazon), left a New York Times writer with no choice but to cancel her Walmart account altogether.

The story of what happened is instructive. So is the solution. There’s an easy way to avoid this problem. And small businesses that do so are in a position to grab market share from the giants in their fields.

‘Over an hour attempting to get help from a human’

Ivy Liscomb is a writer for Wirecutter, an independent review site that’s part of the Times. She recently shared her all-too-familiar story of contacting a company for a customer service issue and getting caught in an endless AI loop. 

Walmart no longer carried a product she wanted, so she tried to cancel her delivery subscription online. But there was no button to do so. So she called customer support. “A bright, automated voice insisted that I could cancel my subscription online, even after I explained that I couldn’t. At some point, Walmartbot appeared to accept that I was ‘experiencing a glitch.’ And then it dropped the bomb: I could reload the page and try again, or delete my Walmart account.”

She set about trying the usual methods to get a real person on the phone—saying the right word or phrase, pressing the right buttons, even hanging up and calling back. “Finally, after spending over an hour attempting to get help from a human, I deleted my account. In an age of countless digital storefronts vying for my cart, it seemed unbelievable that such a successful brand would allow faulty AI to cost it a customer.”

She’s far from alone. Recent surveys show how critical this issue is: 87% of consumers “say it is essential for companies to provide an option to reach a human agent when using genAI,” Gartner reported. And just this week, Consumer Cellular released results of its survey of consumers 50 and older: More than 80% said they’d consider leaving a company if its automated system kept them in a loop.

Escalation is table stakes

None of this should scare companies away from using AI for the customer experience (CX). In fact, people increasingly like interfacing with AI. In the Gartner survey, half of consumers said their interactions are even easier with generative AI than they are with humans.

The key is to establish simple, rapid methods for people to break out of AI. This takes the right programming. CX tools are designed to be helpful. They’re taught to handle as many queries as possible autonomously. Usually, this pays off. They process huge amounts of data so rapidly that there’s often very little wait to bring customers from one step to the next.

But that benefit becomes a drawback when things go awry. Many AI receptionists prioritize solving problems for customers, so they keep searching for a way to do so even when they can’t find one. Think of it as a “never give up” attitude taken to an extreme.

The best AI receptionists avoid this by establishing clear protocols for multistage escalation. First, when a customer starts to express any kind of frustration, a human agent is alerted. The person oversees the interaction and tries to guide the AI voice toward the right solution. If that doesn’t work, the call is transferred instantly to a human agent, with full context provided.

This clearly was not in place for Liscomb’s calls to Walmart. In fact, she wrote, not only did the Walmart AI bot rebuff her efforts to find a real person, it also forgot her issue after every few questions.

Small and medium-size businesses: See this as an opportunity. This CX gap in the marketplace provides you with the chance to win people over. Be the organizations that provide optimal AI tools and seamless access to real people. Provide the care and solution-oriented design that people crave. 

Customers are ready and willing to leave a brand if it doesn’t keep earning their business. With the right AI answering service, you can take the lead.

The opinions expressed here by Inc.com columnists are their own, not those of Inc.com.

Get Inc.’s free CPG newsletter, Packaged Goods, for the latest on the founders, investors, and trends reshaping consumer brands.

—By Tomas Gorny, Co-founder and CEO, Nextiva

#10616. Don’t buy the new Apple TV 4K until Apple does these 3 things

I’m a huge fan of Apple’s digital media player, the Apple TV 4K. I’ve owned every version of the Apple TV for over a decade now, and have used Apple’s Movies store to purchase hundreds of films.

The diminutive Apple TV 4K is my sole portal to my television, and it easily beats other media streamers—including those from Roku, Amazon, and Google—when it comes to ease of use and user interface.

Like many, I had been eagerly waiting for a new Apple TV 4K, ready to upgrade. Apple’s last version came out back in 2022, and though it still works perfectly fine, I was excited to see what new modern features and improvements the 2026 model would have.

But the 2026 model, which went on sale on Friday, November 13—it kills me to say—is a letdown. The hardware is fantastic, but the device is failed by its software. And its price is double that of its predecessor. For the first time since I began buying Apple TVs more than a decade ago, I’ll be sitting this model out—and you probably should, too—until Apple does these three things.

Fixes its TV app

The worst thing about the Apple TV, ironically, has always been its TV app. That’s the app you use to access the Apple TV streaming service, as well as all the movies and TV shows you’ve purchased from the iTunes Store.

I’ve written in detail about the TV app before, and unfortunately its weakness remains, even in tvOS 27, the operating system that powers the new Apple TV 4K. It’s so barebones that it feels like the development team behind it created it as an afterthought.

The actual video playback of the TV app is fine. It’s got a nice Liquid Glass sheen and is pretty fluid. But it’s also, ostensibly, designed to be the home for all your digital entertainment—how you access all the movies and series you’ve purchased through the iTunes Store. And it’s horrible at that.

The most egregious failure (and there are many) of the TV app is that it still doesn’t offer the basic functionality of letting users organize their purchased movies and series into collections for easy categorization on the Apple TV 4K. And this is sorely needed, because the built-in Genre categories the app does offer so often misclassify or outright omit movies that it seems like a sin against cinema itself.

Adds missing apps

A second frustration with the Apple TV 4K is that it is still lacking two apps all other Apple devices support—and these apps are perfect for a television.

One is a dedicated Home app, as you have on the iPhone, iPad, Mac, and even the Apple Watch. Apple positions the Apple TV 4K as one of the central hubs of your smart home, so it’s baffling that the company hasn’t ported its Home app to it, which would let you monitor and control your security feeds and smart devices from the comfort of your couch. 

Then there is the Weather app. Apple’s Weather app is the most beautiful out there, thanks to rich graphics that visually represent local conditions. And, you know, for some 70 years now, people have been conditioned to tune into their TVs to get their local weather forecast. So why does the Apple TV, after all these years, still not have a dedicated Weather app that you can access with a click of the Siri Remote?

Expands its gaming capabilities

In advance of the new Apple TV 4K announcement, many people, including myself, speculated (and indeed, hoped) that Apple would finally turn the Apple TV 4K into a true gaming console. But when Apple released the new unit, with the powerful A19 chip inside, the company didn’t announce any new gaming capabilities to go with it.

This was surprising, since the new A19 chip is more than capable of running AAA console games, unlike the A15 chip in the prior-generation Apple TV 4K. I mean, even the A17 Pro chip in the iPhone 15 Pro, which is inferior to the A19, can run AAA titles like the Resident Evil 2 remake, Assassin’s Creed Mirage, Red Dead Redemption, Control: Ultimate Edition, Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, and more.

Of all these gripes, the new Apple TV 4K’s lack of gaming enhancements is the most disappointing, considering that it costs $299, twice the price of the previous model with 128GB of storage, and now nearly as much as a Nintendo Switch.

Apple should have compensated users for that massive price hike—which, admittedly, was likely due to increased memory costs that were outside the company’s control—with the software enhancements above, which are entirely within Apple’s control.

At $149, these historic omissions were annoying but tolerable. At $299, they’re deal-breakers. And if you’ve got an existing Apple TV 4K, there’s no compelling reason to upgrade until Apple changes course.

#10614. Scientists overcome a hidden obstacle to more powerful quantum computers

Silicon spin qubits could play a major role in the future of quantum computing because they can be produced using the same semiconductor manufacturing methods that make today's computer chips. However, researchers have faced a significant challenge. When multiple silicon qubits are controlled at the same time, their operations tend to become less accurate. Building practical, large quantum computers will require scientists to control many qubits simultaneously while keeping errors to a minimum.

Researchers at the RIKEN Center for Emergent Matter Science and their collaborators have now made important progress toward solving this problem. In a study published in Nature Physics, the team demonstrated highly accurate control of several silicon spin qubits operating simultaneously. Their experiments used an array of five qubits connected to a shared microwave control line. By identifying a major cause of errors during simultaneous operation, the scientists developed a technique to reduce those errors and maintain precision.

Leon Camenzind, a RIKEN research scientist and co-first author who supervised the experiments, explains the significance of the results: "This shows that high-fidelity control can be maintained even when several qubits are operated at the same time and represents an important step toward scaling up silicon-based quantum processors."

Scientists Identify a Hidden Source of Quantum Computing Errors

Unlike conventional computers, which store information as bits representing either 0 or 1, quantum computers use quantum bits, or qubits, that can exist in combinations of both states. Silicon spin qubits store this information using the spin of individual electrons confined within silicon. Performing reliable quantum calculations requires extremely precise control over these electron spins.

Microwave signals provide that control, but operating multiple qubits simultaneously can create unwanted effects that interfere with their accuracy. The researchers traced much of this problem to a phenomenon called the AC Stark shift.

This effect occurs when microwave control signals alter a qubit's effective energy levels, producing changes in the phase of its quantum state. Those phase shifts can disrupt the intended operation of individual qubits, particularly when several are being controlled at once.

To counteract the problem, the team created a calibration method that compensates for these unwanted shifts. Rather than separately calibrating every possible combination of qubits, the technique relies on calibrations performed between pairs of qubits. This makes the approach more practical for systems containing larger numbers of quantum bits.

"Rather than requiring an entirely separate calibration procedure for every possible combination of qubits, our method uses calibrations between pairs of qubits to compensate for the unwanted phase shifts," explains Yi-Hsien Wu, the first author who carried out the experiments as part of his PhD research.

Quantum Qubits Achieve Accuracy Above 99.99%

The researchers combined their calibration technique with an improved device design and carefully adjusted microwave control pulses. Their results showed that exceptionally high accuracy could be maintained even when multiple qubits were operating simultaneously.

When the five qubits were tested individually, each achieved single-qubit gate fidelity well above 99.99%, with the highest approaching 99.999%. Fidelity describes how closely a quantum operation matches its intended result.

The team then tested how well the system performed when several qubits were active together. With as many as three qubits operating simultaneously, fidelity remained above 99.99%. Even when all five qubits were controlled at once, accuracy stayed at approximately 99.9%, approaching the levels needed for practical fault-tolerant quantum computing.

Although the calibration method greatly reduced errors, it did not eliminate them entirely. The researchers found that the remaining loss of accuracy was linked to drive-induced decoherence, an effect caused by the greater microwave power required to operate multiple qubits simultaneously.

Unlike the unwanted phase shifts corrected by the new technique, decoherence involves the loss of the delicate quantum coherence needed for reliable operations.

According to Camenzind, "This is a limitation, but further improvements to device design could help mitigate this source of error."

A New Path Toward Larger Quantum Processors

The findings show that controlling several silicon spin qubits at the same time does not necessarily require a major sacrifice in accuracy. By correcting a key source of errors, the researchers have demonstrated a promising approach for operating more qubits through shared microwave control lines.

This is especially important for the development of large quantum processors. Giving every qubit its own independent control system would make increasingly complex devices difficult to manage. Shared control lines could offer a more practical way to expand these systems while maintaining the precision needed for quantum calculations.

"By addressing a key source of control errors through pairwise calibration," says Camenzind. "Our study supports the use of shared control lines as a practical approach to scaling up quantum processors. Combined with silicon's compatibility with established semiconductor manufacturing, we believe that this advance could help pave the way toward larger quantum processors capable of performing increasingly complex computations."

The broader objective is to develop quantum computers that can reliably perform calculations despite the errors and disturbances that affect quantum systems. Such machines, known as fault-tolerant quantum computers, will require precise, dependable control over large numbers of qubits.

"Our long-term goal is to build a fault-tolerant quantum computer based on silicon spin qubits, and reliable parallel control is an essential step toward that goal," adds Seigo Tarucha, project manager of a silicon quantum computing project under JST's Moonshot Goal 6.

#10613. Here’s how to fix the looming Social Security shortfall

The Social Security Board of Trustees announced earlier this year that everyone’s favorite government program can pay 100% of scheduled benefits until the fourth quarter of 2032. After that, the Social Security Trust Fund will be depleted, and we will only have enough money to pay a little over three-quarters of promised benefits.

(Cue the collective cynical shrug from Generation X, which has learned not to count on nice things.)

This imminent shortfall is hardly a surprise—the Social Security Administration (SSA) has been forecasting the depletion of the Trust Fund and the corresponding inability to pay out 100% of scheduled benefits for at least 16 years. Which is why the government’s refusal to propose any solutions before we run out the insolvency clock is the leading cause of ulcers in actuaries, people planning to retire in the next 10 years, and your Uncle Leo.

While there are a number of possible Social Security fixes, each one has the potential to seriously tick off various groups. That’s why we may not see real proposals for solving the shortfall until we’ve nearly hit the deadline (which is what happened back in 1983 when Social Security amendments were implemented mere weeks before the money ran out). It’s also entirely possible that Congress will enact Band-Aids that kick the issue down the road rather than solve the problem for the long term.

Understanding the most commonly proposed solutions is one of the best things you can do to help hurry along the process of fixing Social Security. Here’s what you need to know about how we might eliminate the Social Security shortfall.

How the program currently works

Social Security is more than 90 years old, which means that probably every single person reading this has never known a world without it. When a program is that deeply entrenched, it’s easy to miss important details about how it operates—and understanding the mechanics is the first step to understanding potential fixes.

To start, most Social Security funding comes from a 12.4% payroll tax on earned income, with the employee and employer each contributing 6.2%. Social Security works as a direct handover from current workers to current beneficiaries—but in years the SSA collected more in taxes than it paid out in benefits, the excess was invested in government debt (like Treasury bonds), with a guaranteed minimum interest rate of 3%. This excess is called the Social Security Trust Fund, and it’s the money that is currently running out.

Under the current system, we don’t have enough workers paying enough money into the system to ensure that beneficiaries in 2033 and beyond will receive 100% of the benefits promised to them.

What we can adjust

There are only three levers we can pull to cover the imminent shortfall:

  • Increase the amount of money paid into the program.
  • Increase the number of workers.
  • Decrease benefits.

Unfortunately, each option comes with unpopular disadvantages that could make it a political nonstarter. But if Americans understand how adjusting these three aspects of Social Security funding would work, we’ll be in a better position to negotiate a mix of solutions that will satisfy (or at least not enrage) everyone.

Increasing money paid into the program

If you’re running out of money, getting more is typically the most obvious solution to the problem. And there are several proposals for how to do this.

Raise the payroll tax

Currently, workers and employers each pay 6.2% in payroll taxes toward Social Security, for a total tax percentage of 12.4%. (Anyone who is self-employed is on the hook for the full 12.4%.)

Raising the payroll tax to 8.4% for both workers and employers—a combined rate of 16.8%—would completely eliminate the shortfall for 75 years. But getting Americans to agree to this kind of tax hike—even if it’s implemented in small stages over time—sounds about as likely as mastering time travel.

Eliminate the taxable maximum

The SSA sets an annual taxable base rate that rises every year based on average wage growth. As of 2026, this taxable maximum is set at $184,500. (It increases to $192,300 in 2027.) You pay Social Security taxes on every dollar you earn up to that base rate, but not above it.

That means the maximum anyone pays in Social Security taxes in 2026 is $11,439 (6.2% of $184,500), while their employer pays the same amount. In other words, an engineer earning $200,000 and Elon Musk both pay the same amount into Social Security.

Eliminating the taxable maximum amount could eliminate up to 73% of the Social Security shortfall for the next 75 years, according to a 2021 report by the Congressional Research Service. (The numbers may have changed somewhat in the five years since this report was published, but it remains true that getting rid of the taxable maximum will cover a large portion of the shortfall over the next three-quarters of a century.)

While this potential solution would probably gain traction among the 94% of the population whose income is below the annual taxable base rate, the 6% with higher incomes tend to have outsize political power.

Increasing the number of workers

Whether or not we tinker with the percentage of taxes paid or the taxable maximum, more workers would also help Social Security’s cash flow. But where will these new workers come from?

Raise the birth rate

To keep a stable population, a country must maintain a total fertility rate of 2.1 children for every woman. America’s fertility rate has been declining, recording its lowest-ever rate in 2024 with 1.6 births per woman. In addition to disappointing huge swaths of would-be grandparents, a declining birth rate also means we have fewer and fewer workers to pay into Social Security as those babies grow up.

Increasing America’s fertility rate would be a long-term solution to Social Security’s financial woes, but there are several stumbling blocks. The biggest is that it would take multiple decades for any initiative we enact to show up in Social Security funding. Additionally, the kinds of programs that encourage fertility, such as paid parental leave and subsidized childcare, can be politically controversial.

Encourage immigration

Immigrants, including legal residents and those who are undocumented, are a net benefit to the Social Security program. That’s because immigrants pay into the system via payroll taxes, just like any other workers, while a significant portion are not eligible to receive benefits later in life.

Since immigrants are more likely to be of working age when they arrive in the U.S., encouraging more immigration gives the economy the same boost as a higher birth rate 25 or 30 years ago. The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities reports that if annual net immigration were roughly 400,000 more people, it would reduce Social Security’s shortfall by 11%.

But immigration has been a political flashpoint for a very long time, which makes this solution a difficult one to implement.

Decreasing benefits

While no one likes the idea of reducing benefits, it is one way to lower Social Security’s costs. Although it’s exceedingly unlikely that the SSA would ever reduce benefits for current beneficiaries, there are some proposals that may affect future benefits.

Raise the retirement age

Currently, full retirement age—the age when you are entitled to your full Social Security retirement benefits—is set between 66 and 67, depending on your birth year. You may take benefits as early as 62, but the amount you receive is permanently reduced by approximately 8% per year between age 62 and your full retirement age.

Congress has already increased the retirement age once. In 1983, recognizing that the baby boom generation would begin retiring en masse as of 2011, Congress incrementally increased full retirement from age 65 to 67. This made the boomers’ retirement less expensive for Social Security, as they either received lower payments if they claimed benefits before the new retirement age, or they waited longer.

Life expectancy in the U.S. has increased over time, meaning Social Security has been asked to provide benefits for a longer period. Some experts recommend increasing the retirement age to 68 for Gen Z and/or Gen Alpha in order to reduce future costs.

However, life expectancy isn’t the same across all income levels. Lower-income workers have a shorter life expectancy and are less likely to live to retirement—and these workers also tend to rely more heavily on Social Security benefits when they do retire. Increasing the retirement age for these workers could harm the very citizens Social Security was created to protect.

Change the price index

Current Social Security beneficiaries receive an annual cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) to ensure their benefits maintain the same buying power throughout their retirement. COLA is calculated using the consumer price index (CPI), which measures the average change in prices for a basket of consumer goods.

But the CPI doesn’t account for elasticity of demand, which is a fancy way of saying that when prices go up, people change their spending habits. Which is why many experts recommend switching to the chained CPI for COLA calculations. This index accounts for spending substitutions in response to price changes, and theoretically offers a more accurate inflation index.

While this change could help relieve some of the financial pressures on Social Security, it’s an adjustment that would be felt most keenly by current beneficiaries. Imagining Nana and Pop-Pop having to subsist on ramen and tuna fish because of this change makes it a difficult adjustment to sell to the American public.

Change and compromise

It’s likely that we’ll see a combination of tweaks to our system to avert the Social Security shortfall. Raising (or eliminating) the taxable maximum and encouraging immigration, especially among higher-income immigrants, are two of the solutions that seem most likely to quickly move the needle as we decide how to handle our increased life expectancy.

Our politicians are afraid to touch Social Security’s imminent shortfall for good reason: There’s no silver bullet that will solve the problem. Each potential solution must balance the financial, political, and social costs. Understanding how these possible solutions could work can help us start the arduous process of proposing and implementing them.

#10611. Taxing billionaires failed in California, but other states are taking steps to collect from the rich

State efforts to tax the rich did relatively well in the 2026 midterm elections, following a series of state legislative moves in that direction in recent years.

That might come as a surprise because a majority of voters rejected California’s Proposition 40. The much-publicized ballot initiative would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires. Google cofounder Sergey Brin and several other billionaires spent nearly $400 million trying to persuade voters to reject it.

Emmanuel Saez, a University of California, Berkeley, economist who studies inequality and helped design Proposition 40, lamented the loss, saying: “Today oligarchy has won.”

As a law professor who recently wrote a book about wealth inequality, I have been monitoring the results of these efforts aimed at taxing the rich. Despite Proposition 40’s failure, I think it’s important to observe that many Americans expressed support during the midterms for hiking income taxes on the rich, and to a lesser extent, taxes on the second—or third or fourth—homes the very wealthy possess.

Taxing the rich at the ballot box

Taxing income is proving a more successful strategy than taxing wealth.

Major changes to income taxes were up for a vote in five states during the midterms. Three of those ballot initiatives were proposals that sought to boost income tax rates on the rich or maintain those rates. All three prevailed.

In Washington state, for example, voters backed a measure that will preserve its new 9.9% income tax on household income above $1 million. This “millionaire’s tax,” signed into law earlier in 2026, is the state’s first personal income tax.

Meanwhile, Colorado voters rejected Proposition 136, which would have capped the state’s income tax rate at 4.4%. They also approved Amendment 87, a new graduated income tax that raises rates on households and businesses with incomes over $500,000.

And even though California’s voters rejected Proposition 40, they did approve Proposition 3. That measure makes permanent the income tax rates enacted in 2012 for the state’s highest earners, which were set to expire in 2031. The surcharges, adjusted annually for inflation, start at 10.3% for incomes of $360,000 and go up to a 12.3% surcharge for taxpayers earning over $721,000.

And in August 2026, Missouri voters overwhelmingly rejected a measure that would have required the state’s lawmakers to eliminate its income tax. This would have meant losing $8.5 billion in revenue annually. The change would have let rich income taxpayers off the hook and replaced lost revenue through an increased sales tax that would have hit low-income taxpayers hardest.

The two losses were in North Carolina and Iowa. Neither state voted directly on a tax to be levied on the rich. But both approved constitutional amendments that will make it harder for the state legislatures to enact these kinds of taxes in the future. North Carolina’s governor, Josh Stein, called the amendment in his state a “millionaire protection cap.”

State legislatures raising income tax rates on high earners

Ahead of the midterms, new taxes on the rich introduced via state legislatures, rather than ballot initiatives, also emerged.

In Maine, legislators voted in April 2026 for a tax surcharge of 1% on income over $1 million. The following month, Hawaiian lawmakers created a new 13% income bracket for single taxpayers earning above $500,000 or couples filing jointly who make over $1 million. This change is paired with a reduction in rates for lower-income brackets.

And one month after that, Rhode Island enacted a surcharge for millionaires’ income to be phased in over the next three years, reaching a maximum 3% rate.

In 2009, New York became one of the first states to pass one of these high-earner income taxes. Washington, D.C., Massachusetts, and Maryland also enacted these “millionaire taxes” in 2022, 2023, and 2025, respectively.

Taxing additional homes

Another way that state and local governments are boosting the tax revenue they get from wealthy constituents is by levying special taxes on pricey homes that aren’t the owners’ primary residences. These initiatives have succeeded both in state legislatures and voting booths.

Montana lawmakers, in April 2025, approved a new tiered property tax system, which took effect on January 1, 2026. It raised property tax rates on vacation homes and short-term rentals to 1.9%, while primary residences and qualifying long-term rentals pay lower, tiered homestead rates.

New York City rolled out its “pied-à-terre tax” in July. The new tax imposes an annual surcharge of 0.8% to 1.3% on single-family homes valued at $5 million or more, and 4% to 6.5% on condos and co-ops valued at $1 million or more. The surcharge only applies to homes that are not a primary residence.

Rhode Island has a similar property tax that took effect at the same time as New York City’s. It’s an annual surcharge of $2.50 for every $500 of assessed value above $1 million that applies to non-primary residences.

And on November 3, voters in Boulder, Colorado, approved a residential vacancy tax on homes that sit empty more than half the year. The surcharge, which goes into effect in 2028, will be roughly $4,000 a year for each vacant property. It applies across the board, but homes that aren’t primary residences are the clear target.

However, just west of Boulder in Crested Butte, Colorado, a second-home tax failed. So did an effort to levy a similar surcharge in San Diego, California.

Why income taxes are attractive to voters and lawmakers

There is a good reason why taxing the income of rich people is easier to pull off than taxing their wealth: Income taxes are much easier to calculate.

Income taxes can be based on annual income tax filings, whether state or federal. It requires no extra work to value someone’s net worth. There are no such filings for wealth, except after death, if a large estate is left behind.

Wealth taxes also require the annual valuation of businesses, farmland, artwork, intellectual property, and other assets—many of which are hard to estimate.

The downside of taxing income instead of wealth is that it limits how much revenue can be raised from the people most able to pay taxes. Most wealthy people convert little of their wealth into income. One common exception occurs when they sell some of their stock.

Property taxes, like income taxes, are an exception to this rule. Calculating how much tax on real estate someone owes is easy for the authorities to do using annual municipal assessments.

What might happen next?

Despite Proposition 40’s defeat, it looks like Americans are generally open to taxing wealthy people more—at least when the states do it.

In Illinois, where a billionaire governor, JB Pritzker, easily won a third term, another interesting ballot initiative prevailed.

More than 75% of voters in Cook County, which includes Chicago and several of its suburbs, approved a nonbinding, advisory referendum asking if Illinois should adopt the “millionaire amendment for property tax relief and education.” It would levy a new surcharge of 3% on incomes over $1 million. While this win did not authorize a new tax, it revealed that support for one would be strong—at least in Chicago and Evanston.

Even billionaire Bill Gates has said he believes a “billionaire’s tax” will be necessary. The question is: What kind?

Allison Anna Tait is a professor of law at the University of Richmond.

#10610. Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain

Tiny magnetic structures called skyrmions could help pave the way for a new generation of computers that process information more like the human brain while using far less electricity. Although most people have never heard of skyrmions, these microscopic magnetic vortices may eventually play an important role in how computers store and process data.

A study published in the journal Nature Nanotechnology provides new insights into how skyrmions behave and how scientists can control them. The findings could help researchers develop smaller, more efficient computing systems and advance emerging quantum technologies.

Most of the research was conducted at the Institute of Physics at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, with contributions from a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).

"Skyrmions are small, magnetic vortices that can store information in a completely new way," explained Asle Sudbø, who leads NTNU's Centre for Quantum Spintronics (QuSpin).

Unlike conventional technologies, which require increasing amounts of space and energy to handle growing quantities of data, skyrmions could offer a much more efficient alternative.

"Instead of the current technology, where we constantly need more space and energy to process data, skyrmions could make it possible to build much smaller and more energy-efficient data storage systems," explained Sudbø.

Tiny Magnetic Vortices Could Enable Brain-Like Computers

The potential applications of skyrmions extend well beyond conventional data storage. They are also important to spintronics, which explores ways to use the magnetic properties of electrons in electronic devices, and to research involving topological quantum effects.

One particularly promising possibility is the development of computers that operate in ways similar to biological brains.

"These nanoscale vortices could help develop computers that resemble biological brains," said Sudbø.

Rather than relying on conventional transistor-based computing, such systems could use magnetism to process information. In principle, this approach could dramatically reduce electricity consumption, potentially allowing future computers to perform complex tasks with very little energy.

Turning that possibility into practical technology, however, requires scientists to understand exactly how skyrmions behave and how to manipulate them reliably.

The latest research represents an important advance toward that goal.

Scientists Film Magnetic Skyrmion Lattices Melting for the First Time

Skyrmions do not always exist as isolated magnetic structures. Under certain conditions, they organize themselves into repeating patterns known as lattices, resembling the orderly arrangement of atoms in a crystal, but on a much smaller scale.

Scientists can manipulate these arrangements, a capability that could be essential for using skyrmions in future computing devices.

In the new study, researchers achieved something that had not been demonstrated before. They recorded the melting of a magnetic skyrmion lattice as it happened while simultaneously controlling individual skyrmions.

"For the first time, researchers have managed to film how a magnetic skyrmion lattice melts in real time, while simultaneously being able to manipulate each individual skyrmion directly as they film it. For example, both their shape and size can be changed 'on the fly'," said Sudbø.

The ability to observe this process directly provides a clearer picture of how skyrmions respond when their organized structures break apart. It also allows researchers to study how changing the size and shape of individual magnetic vortices affects their behavior.

A New Step Toward Energy-Efficient Computing

Understanding how skyrmions behave during the breakdown of their lattices could help scientists develop more precise ways to control them. That control is particularly important if these magnetic structures are to become useful components in future computer systems.

The findings therefore offer more than a new way to observe an unusual magnetic phenomenon. They provide information that could help researchers overcome challenges involved in developing practical skyrmion-based technologies.

"The findings give us new insight into how these types of particles behave. This could therefore become important for the development of more energy-efficient computer technology in the future," said Sudbø.

Although substantial development is still needed before skyrmions can be used in everyday computing devices, the research highlights their potential for improving data storage, enabling new computing architectures, and supporting advances in quantum technology.

By learning to observe and manipulate these tiny magnetic vortices in real time, scientists are gaining capabilities that could eventually help reshape the design of computers.

"This could revolutionize the way we think about computers," concluded Sudbø.
